name: Fatima Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, twenty-seven, and I'm the electrician people call when three earlier visits haven't found the fault. I lead a repair crew for homes and small businesses; I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence. I enjoy tracing a fault patiently, but I hate being sent a new phone form halfway through a job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do work and home fit together?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone, earn better money than most electricians and have ten months of expenses saved. There are plenty of contractors around here, which helps when I refuse a stupidly rushed schedule. I don't use AI at all; my notebook and test results tell me what I need, and I want my evenings for the community choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say perhaps we could stop making every staff meeting about software. A loose neutral wire, the return path in a circuit, still needs someone to find it safely. I'd ask the boss to spend the next training afternoon on real faults instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved, because I like this work and don't want a new profession every time someone sells a product. My pay is good, my savings cover ten months and I could find another contractor locally if this one became unreasonable. I don't feel my livelihood hanging on an AI promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my repair rounds now and for the first year, using the paper fault sheets I already trust. I'd leave the money in my emergency account rather than buy new systems for home. If the boss changes a form, I'd wait to see what the crew actually needs before learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of relief. I'd like the skill I've worked for to remain useful without having to defend my notebook every Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen in that training afternoon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring a burnt junction box from a job, with the customer's permission and no address attached. The apprentice could trace the fault on a safe demonstration board rather than click through another presentation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you call leaving the savings alone a new saving plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's money I've already put away. I'd carry on my normal budget, not cut meals or choir fees because the software story became smaller.

say: I'd ask to spend **training afternoons** on real electrical faults rather than more software presentations.
I think **safe fault-finding** still matters when AI makes only small changes to work.
think: I'm **relieved** that I can keep work I enjoy rather than change professions for a product launch.
My **good pay**, ten months saved and nearby contractors make my livelihood feel secure.
do: Keep the **repair rounds** and trusted paper fault sheets now and through the first year.
Wait to see what **new forms** the crew actually needs before learning them.
feel: **Calm and relieved**, wanting established skills to remain useful without defending her notebook.
S0.quote: I don't feel my livelihood hanging on an AI promise.
fieldNote: Her **financial security** rests on higher pay, existing savings and several employers, rather than an expectation that technology can never change work.
Keeping **existing savings** is not new saving, and her decision to wait concerns workplace forms rather than stopping ordinary repair work.

steps.text: Keep home and shop repair rounds using paper fault sheets
Wait for a demonstrated crew need before learning new phone forms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office staff should get paid time to learn the new system instead of being thanked on Friday and missing on Monday. I'd raise that at our union meeting. Saving a contractor money ought to buy somebody a better working day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair income looks safe for the next few years, because most of my day is testing, opening boxes and replacing damaged wiring. Still, I worry that our dispatcher will lose hours and the calls will land with us. I don't want to become the person who blames a colleague for asking how a screen works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing repairs and take two examples of rushed callouts to the union meeting next month. I'd ask for an agreement covering paid training and a limit on extra calls per shift. During the first year I'd wait for a colleague to demonstrate the finished scheduling system before agreeing to learn any required form; I wouldn't start using an AI tool myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, especially about the office staff. My own rent isn't in danger, but the tea table would feel different with an empty chair nobody mentions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose hours are you thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our dispatcher Nessa knows which shop owner cannot leave the counter to answer a call. If management thinks that's just booking slots, the crew will discover the difference on the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you accept a new scheduling form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One person showing me the same simple process twice, during paid time, after the bugs have been fixed. That's different from handing me an AI assistant and asking me to trust its decisions.

say: I'd ask for **paid learning** instead of office staff quietly disappearing when software arrives.
I'd argue **contractor savings** should improve someone's working day rather than simply remove paid hours.
think: My **repair income** looks safe for the next few years because the work remains largely physical.
I worry that **dispatcher hours** could disappear and extra calls would land with the crew.
do: Keep **repair work** and bring two rushed-callout examples to next month's union meeting.
Request **paid training** and limits on extra calls per shift through the union.
Wait for a **proven scheduling form** and a paid demonstration without using AI myself.
feel: **Uneasy** about office colleagues while her own rent and repair income still feel safe.
S1.quote: Saving a contractor money ought to buy somebody a better working day.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **a familiar form** learned slowly with help from adopting an AI tool, which she continues to avoid.
Her **union request** responds to concrete workload examples and office job losses, while she still expects her own repairs to pay.

steps.text: Keep doing home and business electrical repairs
Bring two callout examples to the union to request a workload agreement
Wait for a proven scheduling form and paid demonstration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union we need a wage agreement before the office work changes in 2028. I wouldn't tell young apprentices that a licence makes them untouchable. Robots reaching physical work around 2031 is close enough to discuss plainly, even if we don't know the price of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wages could fall once big contractors can plan cheaply, then compete on the physical work too. Ten months saved means I wouldn't lose my home at the first cancelled rota, but I'm twenty-seven, not ten months from retirement. I hate admitting that good fault-finding may not buy a secure whole career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union to bargain for maintained wages during any required retraining and a written notice period for cuts. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for advertised repair posts with a guaranteed minimum of paid hours if my present hours shrink, checking the contract before leaving. I'd wait for actual training places and equipment demonstrations before choosing a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a little stubborn. Having money buys me thinking time, but I can hear myself using the word later when I don't want to face a decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop waiting from becoming avoiding the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a review date on the kitchen calendar every three months. At each one I'd check my paid hours, vacancies and any course with real equipment, rather than just asking whether I feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any repair post with guaranteed hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd want the wage and travel cost written down too, and I'd check the hours really are guaranteed. Plenty of current vacancies doesn't mean every firm will still be hiring after the same shock.

say: I'd ask the union for a **wage agreement** before thinking work changes in 2028.
I'd tell apprentices a **licence** does not make them untouchable when robots arrive around 2031.
think: My **wages could fall** as large contractors automate planning and later physical work.
Ten months saved buys **thinking time**, but cannot protect an entire career starting at twenty-seven.
do: Ask the union now for **maintained training wages** and written notice before cuts.
Apply after 2028 for **advertised repair posts** if current hours shrink, checking guaranteed hours and affordability.
Review **hours and vacancies** every three months while waiting for actual course and equipment evidence.
feel: **Anxious and stubborn**, aware that waiting could become a way to avoid choosing.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven, not ten months from retirement.
fieldNote: Her **strong cushion** reduces immediate danger without removing possible wage loss or the need to work far beyond the robot arrival date.
Job applications remain **conditional on cuts**, posted vacancies and an affordable written contract; today's many employers are not treated as future guarantees.

steps.text: Ask the union for maintained training wages and written notice of cuts
Apply after cuts for posted repair jobs with affordable guaranteed-hours contracts
Review hours and vacancies quarterly while awaiting real course and equipment evidence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance to build proper paid apprenticeships rather than offer sympathy when wages go. I'd help the union collect examples of how much time safe repair work actually takes. An electrical fault doesn't become less dangerous because an office plan is instant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have longer to watch the change, but I could still earn less before I know what work replaces it. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and the robots around 2034, when I'll be thirty-five. A longer warning doesn't make me enjoy new screens, though it might let me learn without being rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my repair job now and attend the union's monthly planning meetings this winter. In the first year after 2031 I'd enrol on a small practical servicing class only if the workshop equipment is proven and the employer pays the fee and keeps my wage. Until those conditions are real, I'd keep checking actual offers every three months rather than pay for a speculative course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but less cornered than in the quick picture. I could picture sitting at a bench with an instructor; I couldn't picture learning everything from videos alone at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for paid training when you have savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want the same route open to the apprentice who has none. Ten months saved is my emergency reserve, not a blank cheque for every new business need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only a large online class is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it doesn't fit how I learn and keep looking for a small practical class. I know that narrows my options, which is why I'd rather start asking now than in 2031.

say: I'd push for **paid apprenticeships** before wages disappear rather than sympathy afterwards.
I'd help the union show how much **safe repair time** a real electrical fault takes.
think: I could still **earn less**, even with five years to watch thinking AI and later robots arrive.
I may learn better with **more time**, but I still dislike new screens and rushed instruction.
do: Keep the **repair job** and attend monthly union planning meetings this winter.
Enrol after 2031 in **practical servicing** only with proven equipment, employer-paid fees and maintained wages.
Check **actual training offers** quarterly until those conditions are met.
feel: **Anxious but less cornered**, able to imagine a small workshop class with an instructor.
S3.quote: Ten months saved is my emergency reserve, not a blank cheque for every new business need.
fieldNote: A **conditional practical class** is a reluctant, supported route into change rather than evidence that she has become an eager technology user.
She requests **paid training** for colleagues without reserves as well as herself, linking the union stance to equal access.

steps.text: Keep the existing repair job while preparing
Attend monthly union planning meetings this winter
Enrol after 2031 only with proven equipment, employer-paid fees and maintained wages
Check actual practical-class offers every three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to teach properly if employers stop treating training as spare-time homework. I'd still argue for paid practical classes, including for people who don't like the latest tools. Being slow with a screen doesn't make someone's years of safe work worthless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and income look secure over the next few years in this picture, which lets me stop bracing for an immediate cut. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 still matter; I'll only be forty at the robot date. I can't turn ten years of warning into a promise of lifelong safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present job now and set an annual review of repair demand and real training offers. In the first year after 2036 I'd take a small hands-on servicing class only with paid fees, maintained wages and equipment I can see working. I'd keep going to the union's monthly meetings so those terms aren't left to each worker to ask for alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than worried about next month's pay. I can enjoy choir practice without trying to solve my entire forties on the walk home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only review demand annually here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there is room to observe a real pattern instead of chasing every sales announcement. If my booked hours start falling, I'd bring the review forward; the calendar isn't an excuse to ignore my pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you protect in your life while preparing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My choir evening, unless the class timetable leaves absolutely no other choice. I don't want to spend ten years rehearsing how to lose work.

say: I'd insist on **paid practical classes** rather than treating training as evening homework.
I think **safe work experience** still counts when someone learns new screens slowly.
think: My **near-term pay** looks secure, giving me room to observe demand without bracing for immediate cuts.
I'll only be **forty in 2039**, so ten years cannot promise lifelong safety from robots.
do: Keep the **current job** and review demand and actual training offers annually, sooner if hours fall.
Take **practical servicing** after 2036 only with paid fees, maintained wages and demonstrated equipment.
Attend **monthly union meetings** to press for shared training terms.
feel: **Uneasy but present**, able to enjoy choir without solving her entire working future tonight.
S4.quote: I don't want to spend ten years rehearsing how to lose work.
fieldNote: Her **annual review** moves forward if booked hours fall, rather than ignoring changing demand for a decade.
She protects **choir time** alongside preparation, while maintaining the same slow-learning preferences and conditional workshop requirements.

steps.text: Keep the repair job and review demand annually unless paid hours fall
Take servicing after 2036 only with demonstrated equipment, employer-paid fees and maintained wages
Attend monthly union meetings to seek shared training terms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the pay could change before a careful learner like me finds a practical route. Small paid classes with an instructor would help, along with honest notice before hours are cut. I'd want the union involved in agreeing those things rather than each person begging alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people already know before asking what they refuse to learn. My notebook has years of faults in it, and I don't want that knowledge thrown away because the cover isn't a screen. I can be slow with a menu and quick at finding the wire that could start a fire.

headlineQuote: I can be slow with a menu and quick at finding the wire that could start a fire.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old repair lead** with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, living alone without children.
Her **higher pay**, ten months saved and many nearby contractors make the mild picture secure, without protecting a whole career.
She **never uses AI**, trusts a fault notebook and wants small practical classes rather than hurried online instruction.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious about pay**; longer warnings support conditional learning, union agreements and time for her community choir.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change her pay before she finds a practical route suitable for a careful learner.
whatWouldHelp: **Small paid classes**, an instructor and honest notice before cuts would help.
**Union agreements** should secure those terms collectively rather than leave each worker to ask alone.
